doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: Graphic scores and Mingus
summary: Daley explains his graphic score, how Mingus drew images, and colors marking leads and textures.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I wanted to get to something, before we wrap up. I took advantage last night, because your music was on the stand, and when you went on break I went up and I was looking at it.
You’re welcome to do that anytime.

With a graph of a sort. And is that sort of your blueprint so to speak? And at first I just thought that was interesting. And then coupled with a composed melody that you and Scott eventually would join together on. And I just wanted to comment on that. I thought that was interesting. You sort of invented a way to get your ideas across.

Yeah. Well I didn’t invent that. I mean the graphic scores have been used for years and years and years. Graphic scores are basically an eye concept that many musicians — I mean going back to like Mingus, instead of having an icon like Mingus would just draw a casket and say pass it on. This is what I want. I want you guys to sound like this. And it would be like a casket, you know, something that would kind of like push you into another emotional level. Because the concept in music is to get off of the page. You know what I mean is that you don’t want to sound to the audience like you’re reading the notes on the page. You want to get the notes off the page and assimilate that into your psyche and into your emotional being and then express that as an emotional entity. Not just playing notes off a page and everything. And sometimes in order to get musicians to do that you have to kind of like kick them in the butt, I mean like but Mingus would do that physically too. I mean he would just knock them down if he needed to. So he would do it on that level if it needed to be done that way. But other times he would just draw an image or he would make a political statement, or he was just, you know he was a big, robust, so he would just bully the musician into a position where the musician wanted to fight Mingus back, but you know he couldn’t fight him back physically but he was fighting back via the sounds he was getting out of his instrument and everything. So that’s the way you get to the next level of expression in the music and everything, where people are not expressing you know like C and D and F and everything, they’re expressing emotional sounds and stimulants through each note. And what that graphic score does, it gives the musicians like an outline of who is doing what and everything, and then moving into the melody that I want to use is that rather than just write the melody out without the musicians seeing exactly who is doing what, where, when, with the graphic score. And a prime example of how a graphic score is used is if you see a marching band. If you go see a marching band, that’s how they plot out the marching

band. They plot them out through the graphic score like that where this person’s at the 15 yard line, then he goes this and then he goes up. And this icon comes around and it forms this beautiful whatever, this formation. So the same type of thing with me. I take these icons and I move them along, and then I want a certain textorial formation set up. And the musician sees the exact texture that I want set up. And I want these textures to introduce the next segment of the music that we’re doing, and then part of that introduction to the next segment is going to eventually lead us into a point where we’re going to play a melodic line, based on the textorial distribution of how the instruments are set in place, like I was talking to you last night about how the tuba and the bass saxophone complement each other, the baritone sax and the tenor saxophone complement each other. So that visualization of that, and then it also alerts the musician who will listen for it. Okay I’ve got to listen to him, I’ve got to listen, or whatever. And then there’s certain things in that graphic thing that says who sets the tempo. Who’s going to be the lead voice and everything. And some of the colors, I tell the musicians that if you have to color, if your color is this color then you’re the lead person here. If your color is this then you’re background and everything. So there’s a lot of things in the color concept of a graphic score. But it’s not a new concept and a lot of classical ensembles are using it also, in different sorts of ways. It’s just a new way to notate music so that the musician can get off of the page a lot quicker and get into deeper emotional outbursts of sound than they would just reading C on the third space or whatever.
